title: How does a robot vacuum map your home? (explained simply)
description: How does a robot vacuum map your home on its very first run? This short explains SLAM — the technology that lets robot vacuums build a live floor plan as they clean. You'll see why counting wheel turns alone isn't enough, how a spinning laser measures walls and furniture in real time, and why glass still catches these robots off guard. No jargon, just the real mechanism behind the floor plan on your phone.

scenes.say: Your robot vacuum maps your entire home and finds its way back to the dock. How does it know where everything is?
Here's the paradox: to map the room it needs to know where it is, but to know that it needs the map. Like drawing a map while lost in a dark room.
Counting wheel turns seems like a fix. But one slippery tile, the count drifts. Errors pile up and the robot quickly loses track of where it is.
So instead it fires laser pulses in every direction — that's LiDAR — thousands per second. The pulse travels at a known speed, so return time tells it exactly how far each wall is.
Echo bounces back? Something solid is there. No echo? Clear floor. Each reading marks one small cell on a grid — wall, floor, or not-yet-reached — and the map builds as it moves.

Here's the trick. It senses, estimates position, then — like spotting a familiar corner in a mall — corrects itself. Sense, estimate, correct, repeat. That's SLAM — Simultaneous Localization and Mapping.
The original Roomba just bounced randomly. Today's robots go row by row — like a farmer plowing a field — and only the live map makes that possible.
One thing still fools it: glass. The return beam scatters at the wrong angle — no echo reaches the sensor, so the robot thinks it's open space. <laugh>

visual.sub: No echo = robot thinks: open space

scenes.say: So your vacuum isn't just cleaning — it's constantly sensing where it is and what's around it. Stay curious. Thoma out!

visual.text: Your vacuum is *constantly solving* — where it is and what's around it
